subject: history
subTopic: Daily Life and Households Over Time

questions.content: A historian wants a primary source about daily life in a British town in 1900. Which is the best example?
options: A documentary made in 2020 about Victorian homes
A diary kept by a housewife in 1900
A textbook published in 2015
A historian's essay written in 1990
questions.explanation: A primary source was created at the time by someone who lived through it. The other options were produced long afterwards.

questions.content: Which development did most to reduce the time spent on housework in many homes during the 20th century?
options: Electricity and household appliances
The invention of the printing press
The growth of overseas empires
The spread of compulsory military service
questions.explanation: Electric power allowed washing machines, cookers, irons and vacuum cleaners to become common in homes.

questions.content: During the Industrial Revolution many families left villages to live in growing towns and cities. What is this movement called?
options: Colonisation
Mechanisation
Globalisation
Urbanisation
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the growth of towns and the movement of people into them. Mechanisation means using machines.

questions.content: Which description best fits an extended family household?
options: A single adult living alone
Two unrelated friends sharing a flat
Parents, children and other relatives such as grandparents living together
A parent and one child only
questions.explanation: An extended family includes relatives beyond parents and children. A nuclear family is parents and children only.

questions.content: Why do historians use census records when studying daily life?
options: They contain the private thoughts of every citizen
They are official counts that record who lived in each household, their ages and jobs
They were always written by newspapers
They only describe the richest families
questions.explanation: Censuses give large-scale evidence about households, occupations and population, though not people's feelings.

questions.content: Census records for England and Wales in 1851 showed that, for the first time, more people lived in towns than in the countryside. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: Britain had become a mainly urban society
Farming had completely disappeared
Everyone in towns worked in factories
Living standards were equal across the country
questions.explanation: A majority living in towns means Britain was mainly urban. Farming and rural life still continued, and conditions varied greatly.

questions.content: In a fictional town the average household had 5.2 people in 1850 and 2.4 people in 2000. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: Homes became smaller than they had been
Fewer people lived in the town
More servants were employed in each home
Smaller families and more people living alone
questions.explanation: Falling family size and more single-person households explain a fall in average household size. The other options do not fit the data.

questions.content: A factory owner writes in 1840 that the children in his mill are 'happy and well cared for'. What is the main limitation of this source for a historian?
options: It is too old to be useful
It was written in the same year as the events
The owner had a reason to present his factory in a good light
It mentions children
questions.explanation: Provenance and purpose matter. An owner defending his business may not give a fair account of working conditions.

questions.content: In a fictional country, a typical household spent 60% of its income on food in 1900 and 15% in 2000. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: People ate much less food in 2000
Food took a much smaller share of household budgets, leaving more money for other things
Food was more expensive in 2000
Incomes fell between 1900 and 2000
questions.explanation: A smaller share spent on food usually means incomes grew faster than food costs, so more could be spent on other goods and leisure.

questions.content: Why did the building of sewers and piped clean water in 19th-century cities improve daily life?
options: It reduced water-borne diseases such as cholera
It made factories run faster
It raised the price of housing
It ended the need for doctors
questions.explanation: Dirty water spread cholera and typhoid. Clean water supplies and sewers cut deaths from these diseases.

questions.content: Which is the best example of continuity, rather than change, in daily life between 1850 and today?
options: Households using electric lighting
Most people travelling by train
Children attending school until their mid-teens
Families gathering to share meals and celebrate religious or cultural festivals
questions.explanation: Shared meals and festivals have continued over time. The other options describe changes that arrived during the period.

questions.content: Which was an effect of the First World War on the daily lives of many British women?
options: Women were banned from paid work
All women moved to the countryside
Many took jobs in factories, transport and offices that men had done
Housework was shared equally with men
questions.explanation: With millions of men serving in the forces, women filled many jobs, including in munitions factories.

questions.content: Why can one diary not describe daily life for everyone in a society?
options: Diaries are always false
It shows only one person's experience, which depends on their class, gender and place
Diaries are never written in the past
Diaries only describe weather
questions.explanation: Experience varied widely. A single source is one viewpoint and must be compared with others.

questions.content: Source A is the diary of a wealthy woman in 1880 who writes that servants make daily life easy. Source B is a report describing eight people sharing one room in a poor district of the same city. What is the best conclusion?
options: Daily life in the same city differed greatly by social class, and neither source alone is typical
Source A is wrong and Source B is right
Both sources show that everyone lived in poverty
Both sources prove that servants were unnecessary
questions.explanation: Sources can both be accurate yet show different groups. Good historians combine them to build a fuller picture.

questions.content: A historian claims 'washing machines freed women from housework'. Which evidence would best challenge this claim?
options: A photograph of a new washing machine
A list of washing machine makers
A diary entry praising a neighbour's garden
Time-use surveys showing that hours of housework fell much less than expected
questions.explanation: Rising standards of cleanliness meant that time saved on one task was often spent on others. Surveys of how people used time test the claim directly.

questions.content: Which was a long-term consequence of rapid urban growth in 19th-century Britain?
options: A fall in the number of towns
An end to factory work
Growing pressure for public health laws, sewers and clean water
A return of most families to farming
questions.explanation: Overcrowded towns and epidemics such as cholera led to reforms, including the Public Health Act of 1848.

questions.content: Which argument best explains why the refrigerator is historically significant for daily life?
options: It was invented by one person
It changed how food was stored and bought, cut food poisoning and affected very many households for decades
It looks modern
It was expensive when first sold
questions.explanation: Significance is judged by how many people were affected, how deeply, and for how long.

questions.content: A 1950s advertisement shows a smiling woman delighted with a new kitchen appliance. How should a historian use it?
options: As evidence of the ideals and marketing of the time, not proof of typical home life
As proof that all women enjoyed housework
As useless because it is an advert
As a reliable census record
questions.explanation: Adverts show how products were sold and what ideals were promoted. Their purpose means they are not a balanced record of reality.

note:
## What this topic covers
Daily life means the ordinary routines of people in the past: where they lived, what they ate, how they worked, how they spent free time and how families were organised. Historians study it to understand how change in politics and technology affected normal people, not only rulers and generals.

## Key changes over time
- **Urbanisation**: during the Industrial Revolution many people moved from villages to towns for factory work. The 1851 census in Britain showed that, for the first time, more people lived in towns than in the countryside.
- **Housing and health**: early industrial towns were often overcrowded, with poor sanitation. Epidemics such as cholera led to reforms, including the Public Health Act of 1848, and later to sewers and piped clean water.
- **Technology in the home**: electricity brought lighting, irons, cookers, refrigerators and washing machines to more homes during the 20th century. This changed how food was kept and how much physical work housework needed.
- **Family and household size**: households tended to become smaller over time, with more people living alone or in nuclear families (parents and children).
- **Women's lives**: during the First World War many women took on jobs in factories, transport and offices. Over the 20th century more women entered paid work, though attitudes and pay changed slowly.
- **Social class**: in the same town, a wealthy family with servants and a poor family sharing one room lived very differently. Never write about "the Victorians" as if everyone had the same experience.

## Continuity and change
Strong answers show both. Technology and housing changed greatly, but family bonds, shared meals and festivals continued. Ask: what changed, what stayed the same, and for whom? Also consider the pace of change: some changes were gradual and others, like wartime work for women, were sudden.

## Sources for daily life
- **Primary sources**: diaries, letters, photographs, census records, adverts, household bills.
- **Secondary sources**: textbooks and documentaries written later.
Always consider origin, purpose, content, value and limitations. A census gives numbers but not feelings. A diary gives feelings but only one person's view. An advert shows ideals, not typical reality.

## Worked example
A fictional town had an average household size of 5.2 in 1850 and 2.4 in 2000. The fall is (5.2 - 2.4) / 5.2 = 0.538, about 54%. A good explanation would link this to smaller families and more people living alone, then check it with other sources.

## Common mistakes
- Treating one person's diary as typical of a whole society.
- Describing change without saying when, how much or for whom.
- Forgetting that some groups, such as the poor, left fewer written records.

## How this is examined
Questions give you short sources, such as an extract from a diary, a statistic or an image description. You are asked to identify what it shows, judge its value and limitations using its origin and purpose, compare two sources, and explain change or continuity. Extended tasks ask you to evaluate how far daily life changed, supporting each point with specific evidence.

Exam tip: Always name the group of people your evidence is about and comment on the source's purpose before you decide how much to trust it.

flashcards.back: Evidence created at the time of the events, for example a diary, letter, census return or photograph.
The growth of towns and the movement of people from the countryside into them.
Nuclear: parents and children only. Extended: also includes relatives such as grandparents, aunts and uncles.
Official population counts that record households, ages and jobs. They show large-scale patterns but not people's feelings.
British law that began reform of sewers, water supply and sanitation after cholera epidemics in crowded towns.

flashcards.front: Effect of WWI on women's work
flashcards.back: Many women took jobs in factories, transport and offices while men served in the forces.
Change: what is different over time. Continuity: what stays the same. Good answers give examples of both.
Origin, Purpose, Content, Value, Limitations: a checklist for judging a source.
Daily life varied hugely between rich and poor in the same place, so one source cannot show everyone's experience.

subject: history
subTopic: Art, Literature and Culture as Evidence

questions.content: A painting from 1850 shows a street scene. What can it show a historian?
options: Exactly what every person in the city thought
Clothing, buildings and attitudes, as seen by the artist
Nothing, because paintings are always invented
The census figures for the town
questions.explanation: Art gives a viewpoint on how people dressed and lived, but it is selected and interpreted by the artist.

questions.content: What is the main purpose of a propaganda poster?
options: To persuade people to think or act in a particular way
To record the weather
To list laws in detail
To provide neutral statistics
questions.explanation: Propaganda is designed to influence opinion, for example to recruit soldiers or support a government.

questions.content: A novel published in the 1840s describes poverty in a large city. For a historian studying that decade, it is best described as which kind of source?
options: A secondary source written long afterwards
A census record
A source with no value because it is fiction
A primary source for attitudes of the time, written by someone living then
questions.explanation: Fiction written at the time is a primary source for ideas and attitudes, though it is not a factual record.

questions.content: Which of these is a cultural artefact?
options: A tax law
A river
A folk song passed down through a community
A battle plan
questions.explanation: Songs, stories, art and clothing express the culture of a group and can be used as evidence.

questions.content: What does 'bias' mean when judging a source?
options: Being written in the past
Leaning unfairly towards one side or viewpoint
Being very long
Having a title
questions.explanation: A biased source favours one viewpoint. Bias does not make a source useless but affects how it should be used.

questions.content: A 1915 poster shows a smiling soldier urging men to enlist. What is the best statement about its value?
options: It shows what the government wanted people to do, not how soldiers felt
It proves that all soldiers were happy
It is useless because it is a poster
It shows exactly what the front line looked like
questions.explanation: Its purpose was recruitment. It is valuable evidence of government aims and methods but not of soldiers' real experience.

questions.content: Wilfred Owen served as a soldier in the First World War and wrote poems about it. Why are his poems valuable evidence?
options: They are official government statistics
They were written a century later
They prove how every soldier felt
They record a soldier's first-hand impressions of the war
questions.explanation: A soldier-poet offers an eyewitness view. It is still one person's emotional account, so it is not proof for all soldiers.

questions.content: The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s is best described as which of the following?
options: A military campaign in the First World War
A change of government in Britain
A flowering of African American art, music and literature centred on Harlem in New York
A scientific discovery
questions.explanation: Writers, musicians and artists in Harlem expressed African American identity and gave historians a rich cultural record.

questions.content: The Bayeux Tapestry was made in the years after the Norman Conquest of 1066. Why must historians be careful when using it?
options: It is too colourful to be real
It was made on the Norman side and presents events from a viewpoint favourable to them
It is too short to be useful
It is a secondary source written in the 20th century
questions.explanation: Provenance matters. The people who commissioned and made it affected what it showed and how.

questions.content: In the OPCVL method for judging a source, what does the 'P' stand for?
options: Purpose: why the source was created
Population
Politics
Position in a museum
questions.explanation: Origin, Purpose, Content, Value and Limitations. Knowing purpose shows why a creator chose what to include.

questions.content: Protest songs became popular during the US civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s. What can a historian learn from them?
options: The exact number of marchers on each day
The names of every senator
Nothing, since music is not evidence
The mood, values and demands of people who took part in the campaign
questions.explanation: Songs show attitudes and shared identity. They are weaker evidence of precise facts such as numbers.

questions.content: A student says: 'This newspaper article is biased, so it is useless.' Which reply is most accurate?
options: Biased sources should always be ignored
Only unbiased sources have any value
Bias can itself be useful evidence about the writer's views and the audience
Bias only appears in modern sources
questions.explanation: A biased source can reveal attitudes and propaganda methods. Historians use it with care rather than throw it away.

questions.content: Soviet art of the 1930s often showed smiling workers and heroic leaders. Why is this useful to a historian?
options: It proves that factories were pleasant places
It shows how the state wanted society to be seen and which ideals it promoted
It gives accurate figures for production
It shows the opinions of Soviet critics
questions.explanation: State-sponsored art was used for propaganda. It tells us about official ideals, not actual conditions.

questions.content: Two sources describe the same parade. A government film shows enthusiastic crowds, and a private diary describes people attending out of fear. What is the best approach?
options: Cross-reference both with other sources and consider each source's purpose
Believe the film because it shows images
Believe the diary because it is handwritten
Ignore both and rely on memory
questions.explanation: Comparing sources and checking their purposes helps reach a balanced judgement.

questions.content: A British newspaper cartoon from 1900 shows a foreign leader as a monster. How can a historian best use it?
options: As proof that the leader was cruel
As a photograph of the leader
As a neutral report of events
As evidence of attitudes and stereotypes among the newspaper's readers, not of the leader's real character
questions.explanation: Cartoons exaggerate to make a point. They show the opinions the paper expected its audience to share.

questions.content: In a country with strict censorship, published novels contain no criticism of the government. What can a historian reasonably infer?
options: That everyone supported the government
That novels were not read
Little about public opinion, because censorship limited what could be published
That the government was unpopular
questions.explanation: Absence of criticism may result from censorship. Other evidence, such as private letters, is needed.

questions.content: Which response best evaluates the claim 'Art tells us nothing reliable about the past'?
options: The claim is entirely correct
Art can mislead about facts but is valuable for attitudes, values and what creators or patrons wanted to show
Art is the most reliable source of all
Only photographs count as evidence
questions.explanation: A balanced answer weighs limitations and strengths and links them to the question being asked.

questions.content: A historian describes a whole society using three paintings, all commissioned by wealthy patrons. What is the main weakness?
options: The sample is unrepresentative, since the paintings reflect the tastes and interests of the elite
Three is too many
Paintings cannot be dated
Wealthy people never owned art
questions.explanation: Patrons chose what was painted. Ordinary people were rarely shown, so conclusions about everyone are unsafe.

note:
## Why culture matters to historians
Historians use more than official records. Paintings, novels, poems, songs, films, posters and cartoons all tell us something about what people valued, feared and believed. This kind of evidence is called cultural evidence. It is especially useful for attitudes and emotions, which statistics cannot show.

## Types of cultural evidence
- **Visual art**: paintings, sculptures, tapestries, photographs and cartoons show clothing, buildings and how people wanted to be seen. They are chosen and shaped by the creator.
- **Literature**: novels, plays and poems written at the time reveal ideas and concerns. A novel is not a factual record, but a primary source for attitudes. The poems of First World War soldier-poets such as Wilfred Owen give an eyewitness impression of war.
- **Music**: songs, such as protest songs in the US civil rights movement, express shared hopes and anger.
- **Propaganda**: posters, films and state-approved art try to persuade. The Soviet state of the 1930s promoted pictures of heroic workers. These show official ideals, not everyday reality.
- **Movements**: the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s was a flowering of African American art, music and literature in New York that expressed identity and challenged stereotypes.

## How to judge cultural sources
Use OPCVL: Origin, Purpose, Content, Value, Limitations.
- Who made it, and who paid for it? The Bayeux Tapestry was made after the Norman Conquest of 1066 and presents events from a viewpoint favourable to the Normans.
- Why was it made: to persuade, entertain, record or protest?
- What is shown, and what is left out?
- Is the creator's bias useful? A biased source is not useless. It can reveal the opinions the creator wanted the audience to hold.

## Representativeness and censorship
One painting or song cannot represent a society. Wealthy patrons paid for most art, so the poor appear less often. Under censorship, such as in states that controlled publishing, the absence of criticism does not show that people agreed. It may show that criticism was not allowed.

## Worked example
Source: a 1915 recruitment poster shows a smiling soldier. Content: a cheerful volunteer. Purpose: to persuade men to enlist. Value: shows methods used by the government and the images of bravery it promoted. Limitation: does not show the reality of the trenches. A soldier's poem could be used alongside it to give a contrasting view.

## Common mistakes
- Saying 'the source is biased so it is useless'.
- Treating a painting as a photograph.
- Judging only by content and ignoring who made it and why.
- Generalising about a whole society from one source.

## How this is examined
You are usually given two short sources, such as a poster and a poem, or a cartoon and a diary. Questions ask what each shows, how reliable each is given origin and purpose, and how useful each is for a specific enquiry. Longer answers ask you to compare them and reach a supported judgement about how far they agree.

Exam tip: Judge usefulness for the question asked. A poster can be useless for finding soldiers' feelings but excellent for finding government methods of persuasion.

flashcards.back: Art, literature, music, film and other creations that show the attitudes and values of a society.
Material designed to persuade people to think or act a certain way, often one-sided or exaggerated.

flashcards.front: Does bias make a source useless?
flashcards.back: No. Bias can reveal the creator's views and the opinions they wanted the audience to hold.
Origin, Purpose, Content, Value, Limitations: steps for evaluating a source.
1920s flowering of African American art, music and literature, centred on Harlem in New York.
British soldier-poet of the First World War whose poems give a first-hand but personal view of the war.
Embroidered account of the Norman Conquest of 1066, made from the Norman viewpoint.

flashcards.front: Why can censorship limit a source?
flashcards.back: Silence about criticism may mean it was not allowed, so you cannot assume that people agreed.
Whether a source reflects the wider society. One painting or song may reflect only the creator or patron.

subject: history

questions.content: In which year were the first modern Olympic Games held in Athens?
questions.explanation: The first modern Olympics took place in Athens in 1896, inspired by ancient Greek games.

questions.content: Which technology brought news and entertainment into many homes during the 1920s?
options: Radio
The internet
The smartphone
Satellite television
questions.explanation: Radio broadcasting spread in the 1920s, and families could listen to music and news at home.

questions.content: What does 'leisure' mean?
options: Working hours in a factory
Time spent in school
Military service
Free time used for activities people choose to do
questions.explanation: Leisure activities include sport, music, cinema and hobbies.

questions.content: The Football Association, founded in England in 1863, was created mainly to do what?
options: Organise the first World Cup
Train professional referees abroad
Agree common rules for football
Replace rugby
questions.explanation: The FA created standard rules so that clubs could play each other under the same laws.

questions.content: What is 'popular culture'?
options: Only the art in museums
Music, film, sport, television and fashions enjoyed by large numbers of ordinary people
Laws passed by governments
Religious texts
questions.explanation: Popular culture is mass entertainment and everyday trends, as opposed to elite or formal culture.

questions.content: Why did leisure time increase for many British workers during the 19th century?
options: Laws limited working hours, wages rose and public holidays were introduced
Factories closed down
Families moved abroad
Children took over adult jobs
questions.explanation: Reforms, trade union pressure and the Bank Holiday Act of 1871 gave more time off for many workers.

questions.content: Why was the 1936 Berlin Olympics important to the Nazi regime?
options: It was boycotted by all countries
It was held in secret
It was the first Games ever
It was used to present a positive image of Germany and promote its ideas
questions.explanation: The regime put on a large display, but Jesse Owens' four gold medals challenged its claims of racial superiority.

questions.content: The United States led a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics and the Soviet Union led a boycott of the 1984 Los Angeles Games. What do these events show?
options: Sport and politics are separate
The Olympics were cancelled
Cold War tensions affected sport
Both events were held on the same day
questions.explanation: The boycotts show how superpower rivalry spilled into international sport.

questions.content: At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, medallists Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists on the podium. What were they protesting about?
options: Rules about doping
Racial inequality in the United States
The price of tickets
The location of the Games
questions.explanation: Their gesture drew attention to racial injustice and the civil rights struggle.

questions.content: What was 'ping-pong diplomacy' in 1971?
options: An American table tennis team visited China, helping to ease relations between the two countries
A war between two table tennis clubs
A ban on sport between nations
A trade deal between Japan and Britain
questions.explanation: The exchange of players was a first step before official political contact.

questions.content: In a fictional country, weekly cinema attendance was 30 million in 1940 and 15 million in 1960. During the same period, television licences rose from 0.1 million to 10 million. What is the percentage fall in cinema attendance, and what is its most likely cause?
options: 15%, the rise of radio
50%, the invention of cinema
30%, the fall of television
50%, the rise of television
questions.explanation: (30 - 15) / 30 = 0.5, so a 50% fall. The rapid growth of television in the same period offers a likely explanation, though other factors may also matter.

questions.content: Rock and roll spread rapidly among teenagers in the 1950s. Which combination best explains its spread?
options: It was banned in every country
It was only played in concert halls
Radio, records and television reached young audiences who had more spending money
It was invented in 1850
questions.explanation: Mass media and growing teenage spending power helped new music spread quickly.

questions.content: Early rules of amateurism in some sports required that players were not paid. What effect did this often have?
options: It made sport cheaper for everyone
It favoured people wealthy enough to play without pay and excluded many working-class players
It banned wealthy players
It ended all competitions
questions.explanation: Unpaid play was easier for those with independent income, which linked sport to social class.

questions.content: In 1995 South Africa hosted and won the Rugby World Cup soon after the end of apartheid. Why is this event considered historically significant?
options: It was used to promote national unity in a divided society
It was the first rugby match ever played
It ended the Cold War
It proved sport has no political effects
questions.explanation: President Nelson Mandela supported the team, and the event became a symbol of reconciliation, though it did not solve all inequalities.

questions.content: A student writes: 'Sport is separate from politics.' Which evidence best challenges this claim?
options: The rules of football
The number of teams in a league
The size of a stadium
The 1936 Berlin Games, the 1968 podium protest and the 1980 and 1984 boycotts
questions.explanation: These examples show governments and athletes using sport for political messages.

questions.content: A newsreel film of the 1936 Olympics was made by the German state. How should a historian use it?
options: As a reliable neutral report
As worthless because it is a film
As evidence of how the regime wanted to be seen, but not as a neutral record
As proof that no one criticised the regime
questions.explanation: State-made films serve propaganda purposes. They are valuable for studying the regime's methods and aims.

questions.content: Which feature of leisure shows continuity between 1850 and today?
options: Television is the main form of entertainment
Sport and music remain ways for communities to gather and share an identity
Everyone has the same amount of leisure time
Cinema is the only popular entertainment
questions.explanation: Social activities such as sport and music have lasted, even though the forms and technology have changed.

questions.content: Which statement best explains how football spread across the world in the 20th century?
options: British workers, sailors and traders carried the game abroad, and international bodies such as FIFA (1904) and the World Cup (first held in 1930) organised it
It was spread by one inventor
It spread only through military conquest
It was banned in most countries until 1990
questions.explanation: Several factors interacted: contacts through trade and empire, then organisation through FIFA and international tournaments.

note:
## Sport, leisure and popular culture
Leisure is time people spend on activities they choose. Sport, music, cinema, radio and television can show how ordinary people lived and what they valued. Popular culture is the entertainment and trends enjoyed by large numbers of people. Historians study it to learn about society, class, gender, identity and politics.

## Key developments
- **More free time**: during the 19th century in Britain, laws limited working hours and the Bank Holiday Act of 1871 created public holidays. As wages and free time grew, so did leisure industries, such as seaside holidays and organised sport.
- **Organised sport**: the Football Association (1863) set common rules. FIFA was founded in 1904 and the first World Cup was held in 1930. The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens in 1896.
- **Mass media**: cinema became popular early in the 20th century, radio in the 1920s and television in homes after the Second World War. Each new medium reached more people and spread trends faster. Rock and roll in the 1950s spread to teenagers through records, radio and television.
- **Class and sport**: some sports had amateur rules that favoured those who could afford to play without pay, linking sport to social class.

## Sport and politics
Sport is often used for political ends.
- **Berlin 1936**: the Nazi regime used the Olympics to promote a positive image of Germany. Jesse Owens' four gold medals challenged its claims of racial superiority.
- **Mexico City 1968**: Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists on the podium to protest racial inequality in the United States.
- **Moscow 1980 and Los Angeles 1984**: boycotts led by the United States and the Soviet Union show the Cold War reaching sport.
- **Ping-pong diplomacy 1971**: an American table tennis team visited China, helping ease relations.
- **South Africa 1995**: the Rugby World Cup was used to promote unity soon after apartheid ended.

## Worked example
A fictional country had weekly cinema attendance of 30 million in 1940 and 15 million in 1960. Percentage change = (15 - 30) / 30 x 100 = -50%. During the same years television ownership grew from 0.1 million to 10 million homes. A reasonable explanation is competition from television, but also consider other factors such as the cost of tickets or changes in lifestyle. Use evidence, not assumption.

## Using leisure as historical evidence
- Films, posters, newsreels and match programmes show what was promoted. State-made films such as 1930s newsreels serve a purpose, so judge their origin and aim.
- Attendance figures show popularity but not why people attended.
- Remember that leisure differed by class, gender and region.

## Common mistakes
- Saying 'sport and politics are separate' without testing the claim.
- Claiming that one factor, such as television, caused everything.
- Forgetting to mention continuity, such as communities still gathering around sport and music.

## How this is examined
Typical tasks give a source such as a poster, a newsreel description or attendance data. You may be asked what the source suggests about leisure and society, how reliable it is, and what other sources would help. Extended questions ask how far leisure changed or how sport has been used for political purposes.

Exam tip: When asked about causes of change in leisure, name at least two factors, such as technology and rising free time, and explain which was more important and why.

Founded in England in 1863 to agree common rules for football.
FIFA was founded in 1904. The first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930.

Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists on the podium to protest racial inequality in the United States.
US-led boycott of Moscow 1980. Soviet-led boycott of Los Angeles 1984. Cold War tensions spilled into sport.
1971 visit of a US table tennis team to China that helped ease relations between the two countries.
Music, film, sport, television and trends enjoyed by large numbers of ordinary people.

flashcards.front: Why did leisure time grow in the 19th century?
flashcards.back: Shorter working hours, rising wages and holidays such as those created by the Bank Holiday Act 1871.
